questions.question: Nadia snaps linking cubes together to make one solid cube. It is 7 cubes long, 7 cubes wide and 7 cubes high, with no gaps inside. How many linking cubes does she use in all?
questions.explain: A solid cube that is 7 on every edge holds 7 × 7 × 7 = 343 cubes, which is why we write 7³. The exponent 3 says to use 7 as a factor three times; reading it as 'times 3' gives only 21.

questions.question: Ben builds one solid cube out of linking cubes with 5 cubes along every edge, so it is 5 long, 5 wide and 5 high. Which calculation gives the total number of linking cubes in his build?
questions.explain: 5³ means three 5s multiplied together: 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. The one that says 5 × 3 = 15 treats the small 3 as 'multiply by 3', and 5 × 5 = 25 counts only the bottom layer.

questions.question: A solid cube of linking cubes is 10 cubes long, 10 cubes wide and 10 cubes high. The class writes the total as 10³. What does 10³ mean for this build?
questions.explain: The exponent 3 counts how many times 10 is used as a factor: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 linking cubes. The common slip is 10 × 3 = 30, which is not even one layer of the build.

questions.question: Priya has 70 linking cubes in her bin. She builds one solid cube that is 4 cubes long, 4 cubes wide and 4 cubes high, taking only as many cubes as she needs. How many cubes does the build use, and how many are left in the bin?
questions.explain: The build is 4³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cubes, so 70 - 64 = 6 stay in the bin. The one that says 16 used stops at 4 × 4, which is just the flat bottom layer.

questions.question: Which of these amounts of linking cubes can be built into one solid cube with none left over?
questions.explain: A perfect cube is a number written as n × n × n, and 27 = 3 × 3 × 3 = 3³. The one that says 36 is a perfect square, so those cubes make a flat 6 by 6 layer, not a solid cube.

questions.question: Which statement about 2³ and 3² is true?
questions.explain: 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 (a solid cube 2 on each edge) and 3² = 3 × 3 = 9 (a flat 3 by 3 square), so 3² is bigger. The traps are turning 2³ into 2 × 3 = 6 or 3² into 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.question: A cube-shaped storage bin at Ryan's soccer club measures 30 cm along every inside edge. Which calculation gives the space inside the bin, in cubic centimetres?
questions.explain: A cube with 30 cm edges holds 30 × 30 × 30 = 27 000 cm³, which is exactly what 30³ is shorthand for. Stopping at 30 × 30 = 900 covers only one flat layer of the bin.

questions.question: A tub in the math room holds 1000 linking cubes, and the prime factorization of 1000 is 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 5. Can the whole tub be built into one solid cube?
options: No — 1000 is a perfect square instead
questions.explain: Grouping the prime factors as (2 × 5) × (2 × 5) × (2 × 5) gives 10 × 10 × 10, so the tub builds a solid cube 10 on every edge. Saying a cube of 10 is 10 × 3 = 30 mistakes the exponent for a multiplier.

questions.question: For a math fair display, Ava first builds a solid cube that is 4 linking cubes on each edge. She then decides the display looks better as a solid cube 5 cubes on each edge. How many extra linking cubes does she need?
questions.explain: The two builds are 5³ = 125 and 4³ = 64, so she needs 125 - 64 = 61 more cubes. Comparing 25 and 16 uses squares, which count only one flat layer of each build.

questions.question: Noah writes that a solid cube with 6 linking cubes on each edge needs 18 cubes, because he says 6³ = 6 × 3. What is wrong with his thinking?
options: He should use 6 × 6 = 36, one flat layer
questions.explain: Cubing means using 6 as a factor three times: 6 × 6 × 6 = 216. Multiplying by 3 gives 18, which is not even enough for a single 6 by 6 layer of the build.

questions.question: A cube-shaped compost bin in a Vancouver backyard measures 40 cm along every inside edge. The family has 60 000 cm³ of soil to store in it. How much does the bin hold, and does all the soil fit?
options: 1600 cm³, so the soil cannot fit
120 cm³, so the soil cannot fit
80 cm³, so the soil cannot fit
questions.explain: The bin holds 40³ = 40 × 40 × 40 = 64 000 cm³, and 64 000 is more than 60 000, so the soil fits. Using 40 × 40 = 1600 measures only the flat bottom, not the whole solid.

questions.question: A Grade 8 class builds a solid cube 4 linking cubes on each edge, using 64 cubes. They then double the edge to 8 cubes and predict the new build will need twice as many. How many cubes does the new build really need?
options: 128 cubes — exactly twice as many cubes
512 cubes — 8 times as many, not twice
questions.explain: The new build is 8³ = 8 × 8 × 8 = 512 while the old one is 4³ = 64, so doubling the edge multiplies the cubes by 8. The answer 128 doubles only the total and forgets that all three dimensions grow.
